questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The exchange would not be a burden financially or timewise to prepare.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was very easy. They provided it throughout. But be sure to get an overview of all the systems as soon as possible. University of Heidelberg and Heidelberg Studerenwerk are separate institutions, and the latter is the one for most intro, accommodation and student life. Check LSF regularly prior as course descriptions come continuously. Registration for courses differed, find that on LSF:

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I imidatly got my key from Studerenwerk and apartment on arrival. There was a full week of introductions that informed about everything from where to get a bike, courses, student societies, sports and much more. I advise to join all of it, even though some parts may seem boring. It is nice not to miss out on information.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Before going we got a from to choose between cheap/average/high price, all still incredibly cheap (I had an "expensive" for 1850 dkk). The price depends on whether you are in a shared or single drom. However there is scarcity in housing. Exchange students have priority but it is distributed randomly.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: I had my own small kitchen. However most students go to the canteen/Menzas that are at every campus but the one at INF and Marstall are the biggest and best. The food is pretty healthy and cheap. You pay by weight. There are good vegan options and can be to-go in reusable boxed.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: You may be lucky maybe not. Use Studerenwerk for help.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Some was prior. For courses it differes from course to course, so check LSF. You need to mail documents to the main building or bring them yourself. They cannot make your studentcard before that, and you depend on the studentcard for Moodle (their absalon), the library, canteen, local transport and more. So I recommend actually sending it by mail as soon as possible from home. Thay had to make so many in the first week of the semester, that it took at least a week to get it.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could get a lot of help at the offices. However the orientation week is the main place to get help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very successful. Mainly because I really made sure to check LSF regularly and get an overview of the registration process.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Prioritize preprations and getting an overview. The students that had not prepared had a substantially harder time in the beginning compared to me.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The economics students level and courses are very similar to here. The MA students have a mandatory math course, where they thoroughly learn the math that we will probably have learned bit by bit in our courses. So in the beginning of the MA first semester, their math skills were a bit lower than our average, but they caught up. Their econometric skills may be slightly lower than ours, where in the seminars Diff-n-Diff, IV, and Regression Discontinuity were kinda of what was considered the "harder" parts and sufficient, whereas in my experience, the MA level here, like AME, is far beyond that.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Substantially more discussion based leaning and student engagement. The lectures had far more responsibility, freedome and flexibility for the curriculum, assignments and exam wich means that it can be based on the students interests. I did a LOT of presentations as part of my courses.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Advanced Experimental Economics
Applied Methods on Environmental and Development Economics (Seminar)
Politics in Contemporary India
Political Ecology of Urbanization in South Asia
West Punjab: Heratage, Memorilization and Ethnography
International Reserach Seminar: Heritage Conservation in Postcolonial Pakistan

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
All of them. 
Advanced Experimental Economics was far more practical and active that I am used to, where we mainly did the experiments with each other and had to come up with a design. For the seminar, the paper had to replicate another paper and add an element. I found that to be both slightly easier than our seminars, but also a very good starting point which meant that I actually could lean more and do better then if I did not have to base it on another paper.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: It was not unexpected, but to get kitchen equipment and stuff for my felt that I did not bring, I went to the thrift store Bric & Brac and got absolutely everything I needed, which was very cheap.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: On the weekdays at certain hours, students have free local transportation, and you can get a cheap semester card so you can travel all the time in a more extensive area. My rent was incredibly cheap compared to the fact that it was the absolute best location you could imagine, large with a bathroom and small kitchen and my own. Getting to Heidelberg from CPH is also cheap; there is a Flixbus that goes directly during the night, and as DB is known for delays and fuck ups, it is the best option. Since it is free to go for walks, that means that the most amazing parts of Heidelberg is at no cost. As Heidelberg is a very rich city, the prices in supermarkets etc. are in the same arena as CPH, maybe a bit more.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
The main part of Heidelberg's history and beauty. It's no wonder that it is a huge tourist attraction. So beautiful during Christmas, and when I arrived in the start of October, I saw people play beach volley shirtless. You can kayak in the Necker. The Neckerwiese is incredible. Walk philosophweg. Hear about the history. Visit Germany's first prime minister's childhood home. Go to the castle. Go to Christmas markets. Go to private parties at strangers' houses, because that is the nightlife in Heidelberg. Visit Manheim for an urban vibe. Connect with the other Danish exchange students to have a safety net and have each other back.
You can do all kinds of sports at the uni institution Hochschulsports.
https://www.hochschulsport.issw-hd.de/
Be sure to join orientation for this, as the registration is a bit hard and you have to be fast if you want the good spots.
There is a student-led organization for Erasmus students that host event all the time, and every day in the beginning of the semester.
https://www.instagram.com/esn_heidelberg/
Germans are kinda like Danes, and don't really want to meet new people, especially if you are not german speaking. So prioritize getting your social crew with the other Danes and internationals.
There are a ton of cute cafes.
The libraries are nice, but so weird that you cannot bring food or coffee in there, and need a see-through bag to get in. Very frustrating. That's why you can study at Mensa.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The majority of the student life is at Mensa, where you can eat but also have a beer or latte at Marstall the cafe. They also host poetry slams and shit.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: See the above. Go for walks by the Necker or the mountains. It's crazy what is does to not be in such a flat place.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Prioritize making friends in the beginning. Don't prioritize Germans, but the other internationals, they are way more open. Maybe you are one of those people that I was on my first exchange, thinking you are not there to make friends and can do without. No. It can get lonely. You need people to support you. Seek a base with the other danish students. I know you may think you did not go to hang out with danes. Sure, you should also make international and German friends. But they will probably be where you will get a meaningful and trusting relationship easiest, and that is important to have.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: In stores, especially bakeries, they are not foreign-friendly. Practice the basic German terms. You need to use titles for your lectures, and there is more of a hierarchical distance between you in general, but that is mostly a formality. People go to strangers' private parties?? It was so weird initially when I was invited to a friend-of-a-friend-of-a-friends home. But that is normal because their public nightlife is very much like Gothersgade, so hated by most.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: That it was easy as it is so similar. I was not there for a big cultural experience but for a nice and smooth trip. For that it was really nice to go.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Arrive early to get settled and prioritize the orientation week. 
2) Prepare from home
3) Make friends with the other Danes for a saftlyned

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: They are obsessed with Mate.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The beauty of Heidelberg and the pleasure of living a short while in a city where the uni and student life is at the core.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I don't like Mate.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Nope.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
